segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After this I saw four angels standing at the four corners of the earth, holding back the four winds of the earth so that no wind would blow on the earth or on the sea or on any tree.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And I saw another angel coming up from the rising of the sun, holding the seal of the living God, and he cried out in a loud voice to the four angels who had been permitted to harm the earth and the sea,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: saying,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: “Do not harm the earth or the sea or the trees until we have sealed the slaves of our God on their foreheads.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And I heard the number of those who were sealed: one hundred forty-four thousand, sealed from every tribe of the sons of Israel:

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: from the tribe of Judah twelve thousand were sealed, from the tribe of Reuben twelve thousand, from the tribe of Gad twelve thousand,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: from the tribe of Asher twelve thousand, from the tribe of Naphtali twelve thousand, from the tribe of Manasseh twelve thousand,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: from the tribe of Simeon twelve thousand, from the tribe of Levi twelve thousand, from the tribe of Issachar twelve thousand,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: from the tribe of Zebulun twelve thousand, from the tribe of Joseph twelve thousand, from the tribe of Benjamin twelve thousand were sealed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After these things I looked, and there was a great crowd that no one could count, from every nation and from all tribes and peoples and languages, standing before the throne and before the Lamb, clothed in white robes, with palm branches in their hands.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they cry out in a loud voice, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Salvation belongs to our God, who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And all the angels were standing around the throne and the elders and the four living creatures, and they fell on their faces before the throne and worshiped God,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: saying,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: “Amen! Blessing and glory and wisdom and thanksgiving and honor and power and strength belong to our God forever and ever. Amen!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then one of the elders spoke up and said to me,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “These people clothed in the white robes—who are they, and where have they come from?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “My lord, you know.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he said to me,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “These are the ones coming out of the great affliction; they have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: For this reason they are before the throne of God, and they serve him day and night in his sanctuary, and the one who sits on the throne will spread his tent over them.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: They will hunger no more and thirst no more; the sun will not beat down on them, nor any scorching heat,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: for the Lamb at the center of the throne will shepherd them and guide them to springs of the waters of life, and God will wipe away every tear from their eyes.”

notes.note: A seal was a stamp of ownership and protection, pressed on goods or documents to show whose they were. The scene recalls Ezekiel 9, where a mark is placed on the foreheads of the faithful in Jerusalem so that they are spared when judgment falls on the city.

The Greek word is the ordinary term for a slave, a person owned by a master, and the seal as a mark of ownership fits that sense. Most English versions have “servants,” partly because “slave” carries associations from modern history and partly because the Hebrew Scriptures use the equivalent term as a title of honor for those who belong to God. Both points are fair, but “servant” suggests a hired employee, which the word does not mean.

The number is twelve times twelve times a thousand, twelve thousand from each of twelve tribes. Interpreters disagree whether it refers to Jewish believers specifically or is a symbolic picture of the whole people of God. They also disagree whether the uncountable crowd of verse 9 is a second group or the same group seen from another angle; John hears the number and then sees the crowd.

The list does not match any tribal list in the Hebrew Scriptures. Judah, the tribe of the Messiah, stands first instead of Reuben the firstborn; Dan is missing; and Manasseh is listed alongside Joseph, his father, while Ephraim is not named. The reasons for the omission of Dan are uncertain, though ancient and modern interpreters have often linked it to that tribe’s association with idolatry.

The Greek has no verb: literally “the salvation to our God … and to the Lamb.” The word covers rescue, deliverance and, in the Septuagint, sometimes victory; some translators render “Victory to our God.” The traditional rendering is kept, with the sense that deliverance is God’s work and is credited to him.

The word is the usual respectful address to a superior and is the same word used for “Lord” of God and Jesus. Here John addresses one of the elders, so it is not capitalized. Most versions have “Sir,” which is also accurate; “my lord” keeps the possessive pronoun the Greek has and the deference it expresses.

The Greek is a present participle. It may picture people still arriving as the vision unfolds, or it may simply describe the group without reference to time, as in the common rendering “those who have come out.” The following verbs, “washed” and “made white,” are past tense.

The Greek word was an ordinary term for oppressive hardship, the same one used for “great affliction” at Matthew 24:21 and Acts 7:11. “Tribulation” is now widely heard as the technical name of a specific end-time period, which says more than the word itself does. Whether the phrase here points to a single final crisis or to the whole course of the church’s suffering is debated; that is a question of what the phrase refers to, not of what the word means.

Greek has two words that English Bibles usually both translate “temple”: one for the whole complex with its courts, and this one for the building where God dwells. This translation renders the second as “sanctuary” throughout so that the distinction stays visible. Most versions have “temple” here, and standard lexicons allow either.

notes.phrase: will spread his tent over them
notes.note: The verb means to pitch a tent or encamp, and here it takes a preposition meaning “over” or “upon,” not “among.” It evokes the tabernacle, the tent of God’s presence in the wilderness, and the promise that God would shelter his people. Older versions have “dwell among them” and several modern ones “shelter them”; the rendering here keeps both the tent image and the sense of covering.

notes.phrase: They will hunger no more and thirst no more
notes.note: Verses 16 and 17 are woven from the language of Isaiah, without being introduced as a quotation. Isaiah 49:10 promises the returning exiles that they will not hunger or thirst, that heat and sun will not strike them, and that they will be led to springs of water; Isaiah 25:8 promises that God will wipe away tears from all faces. Here the shepherd who leads them is the Lamb.

candidates.reason: Occurs throughout the New Testament for both literal slaves and God’s people; versions split between “servant” and “slave,” and the choice must be uniform across books.
The tent or tabernacle image links John 1:14 with Revelation 7:15, 12:12, 13:6 and 21:3, and versions vary between “dwell,” “shelter” and “tabernacle.”
Recurs throughout Revelation and must be kept distinct from θηρίον (“beast”), which the KJV blurred by using “beasts” for both.
Very frequent in the Gospels, Acts and Revelation, where versions alternate between “crowd” and “multitude” for the same sense.
In Revelation it means to damage or hurt, while elsewhere it means to wrong or act unjustly; the split by sense should be fixed once.
